The C executor is one of the solutions that has been developed in the micro-ROS project. It is designed based on the Logic Execution Time (LET) concept with additional features such as static memory allocation, user-defined callback priority, and executor trigger conditions. Thanks to these features, the C executor improves time and data determinism. While micro-ROS and the C executor have made significant advancements toward bringing determinism to robot applications, there are still areas for improvement. The LET concept is not fully implemented yet and there is no mechanism to handle callback execution overrun. On top of these limitations, the C executor’s lack of enforcement of the LET concept and reliance on user configuration may lead to confusion as there is no provided guidance during implementation. This thesis is part of a larger project of Alten Netherlands, with the goal of gaining more knowledge of ROS2 and its application in the services that they are providing to other companies. A remote-controlled robot arm has been developed by Alten and provided to us as an example. This particular project provides an insightful context for our research on addressing predictability and determinism challenges within the ROS2 framework. While Alten’s project serves as a valuable reference, our research extends to wider applications in ROS2 and Micro-ROS, targeting challenges in real-time systems beyond this specific use case. In our thesis, the advantages and shortcomings of the C LET executor when applied in ROS2 system will be investigated and its limitations will be addressed. In addition, a user guide will be provided to help with implementation details. 2 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Chapter 2 Background Information 2.1 ROS2 ROS2 is designed to support modularity and composability. It achieves this by abstracting away the hardware and communication implementation details as well as providing API in multiple programming languages like C++ and Python. The layer abstraction is visualized in Figure 2.1. At the bottom is the Data Distribution Service (DDS) layer that abstracts the upper layers from the operating systems, the transport layer, the network layer, the data link layer, and the physical layer. It is a data-centric middleware with a publish-subscribe communication pattern. Any DDS vendor can be used, but ROS2 officially supports Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, and Connext DDS. The next layer is the Ros Middleware Interface layer, which provides API to the upper layers for any DDS implementation. The Client Library layer is where most of the ROS2 application models are defined. On top of it is the Client Library Wrapper layer that provides language-specific API to the application layer along with the execution management. Although there are multiple supported programming languages, either officially by ROS2 or by third-party, the focus of this paper will be limited to C/C++ as they are the obvious choices for real-time systems due to their popularity and low level among general-purpose languages. In addition, most research and development on the scheduling behavior of ROS2 is with C and C++. Figure 2.1: Layered architecture of ROS2 The ROS2 application architecture is shown in Figure 2.2. It consists of multiple nodes, each A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 3 responsible for a distinct functionality (e.g. sensor data acquisition, sensor data fusion, motion planning). These nodes can either reside on one processor or be distributed among multiple hosts. Within a node, there are smaller entities, including timer, publisher, subscriber, client and server. The last four entities handle the communication between nodes using the publish-subscribe mechanism. Nodes (i.e. publishers) publish messages on topics, which then are broadcasted to all the nodes (i.e. subscribers) that subscribe to the topic. Once nodes receive a message, a corresponding callback is activated to process the message. The client and server are simply twoway publish-subscribe communication, which also has a service callback and a client callback. The timer is used to activate a timer callback, enabling actions such as periodic data collection from a sensor. Collectively, the communication callbacks and timer callbacks function as tasks within a scheduling model. In ROS2, the management of these callbacks is handled by an executor, implemented within the Client Library Wrapper layer. It is important to clarify that there can be multiple executors within a ROS2 application, and they provide an additional layer of scheduling on top of the operating system scheduler. The executor determines the order in which callbacks associated with the executor will be executed. At the operating system level, callbacks chosen for execution by different executors implemented over the same operating system will compete for processor access based on the scheduling performed by the operating system scheduler. Further details of how the executor manages the callback execution are provided in Section 5. Figure 2.2: Simplified representation of ROS2 application 2.2 Real-time systems and ROS2 Real-time systems are systems that must react within precise timing constraints (also called deadlines) to events in the environments

Real-time capabilities are a key requirement in many robotics systems, especially for safety-critical systems such as industrial manufacturing, autonomous vehicles or medical robots. ROS2 has been developed to satisfy real-time constraints. Although its real-time properties have been vastly improved over ROS1, more effort is still needed for ROS2 to be suitable for real-time systems, where a single deadline miss would cause the system to go into an abnormally unstable state. For those systems, being fast is not enough as they should also 4 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 be predictable. The goal is not to minimize the end-to-end latency but to make it predictable to ensure the tasks can be finished before the application-related deadlines at all times. In ROS2, the main source of unpredictability is the execution management of callbacks. In LET, communication of data between tasks occurs only at predefined periodic instances: reading data (input) at the beginning of the period and writing data (output) at the end of the period. This concept is based on the observation that the behavior of an application only depends on when input is read and output is written instead of when the execution starts and finishes. The duration between the input read and output write is called the Logical Execution Time of a task. The concept of LET is shown in Figure 2.4. To ensure the correctness of the system, the LET of a task must be greater than or equal to the worst-case response time of that task. Figure 2.4: Timing diagram for a task in normal execution model (left) vs LET model (right) By having the output written at a predefined instance, the system timing behavior becomes predictable and as a result, the response jitter is reduced. On the other side, by writing output at the end of the period, the LET model increases the end-to-end latency. Another advantage of the LET model is data consistency, as illustrated in Figure 2.5. Figure 2.5 shows a task chain with only two tasks with different periods running with a preemptive scheduling algorithm. In Figure 2.5(a), each of the task chain instances (differentiated by the colors) has a different end-to-end response time as well as data flow due to the variance in the task execution time. In Figure 2.5(b), by reading input and writing output at the end and beginning of each task period, the task chain response time and data flow become static, but the end-to-end latency of the task chain becomes higher. Figure 2.5: Data dependency between two tasks in a single core with preemptive scheduling in normal model vs LET model 2.5 Context from Alten’s Use Case Alten is a company in technical consultancy and engineering with expertise in ROS and ROS2. To expand their knowledge and technical know-how of ROS2, Alten has initiated several internal 6 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 projects exploring its potential. One example includes the development of a remote-controlled robot arm designed for tasks like picking and placing objects. The project is still in an early stage with the current implementation including a robot arm and a robot hand that can be controlled by a user through a PC. The detailed hardware architecture is illustrated in Figure 2.6. One Raspberry Pi is used to control the robot arm and one Raspberry Pi is used to do camera image processing and control the robot hand. The ROS2 application in the current implementation is minimal, but an example of a more completed ROS2 implementation of the project is presented in Figure 2.7. Figure 2.6: Current hardware architecture of Alten’s use case Figure 2.7: A possible ROS2 architecture of Alten’s use case There are challenges in ROS2 related to predictability and determinism. Such challenges pose a risk as sensor data can’t assure the prevention of robot crashes or human injuries. Unpredictability can emerge from varied sources, such as user applications, ROS2 libraries, or the underlying hardware. Given this, the robot arm example offers valuable context for our research, which addresses the unpredictability within ROS2 framework, particularly in its execution management. By introducing a new predictable executor of ROS2 that can be used in the microcontroller that controls the robot arm, the control and feedback loop can be operated reliably and predictably. It is worth mentioning that while Alten’s use case provides a practical reference, the scope of our research extends beyond this single application. Our work in ROS2 and Micro-ROS targets broader challenges and is relevant in many other scenarios besides Alten’s specific example. Detailed Analysis of ROS2 and Micro-ROS executors: We present a comprehensive examination and description of the latest scheduling models in both the ROS2 C++ executor and the Micro-ROS C executor. This analysis serves as a valuable resource for engineers and researchers working on ROS2 systems. 2. A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 11 Chapter 5 Analysis of The Current Executors in ROS2 and Micro-ROS In this section, the behavior of the C++ executor and C executor of the most recent release (Humble) will be analyzed to identify their effect on their timing performance. 5.1 Default ROS2 Scheduling (C++ executor) In ROS2 applications, nodes and their callbacks are added to executors that control the order of callbacks’ execution. An application can have one executor for all callbacks, or multiple executors with each responsible for a callback group. The executor can be single-threaded with sequential processing or multi-threaded with parallel processing capability. In this section, the scope will be limited to the single-threaded executor version, as the multi-threaded version can also be implemented with multiple single-threaded executors with the advantage of providing more fine-grain control of the task-to-thread assignment. The scheduling algorithm of a single-threaded executor is visualized in Figure 5.1. All incoming messages are stored in queues in the rmw layer, with one queue per callback. A wait set variable is used to store all the callbacks of the executor that is waiting for data. This variable is then passed to a blocking wait function, which is returned only when there is new data arrives or there is a timeout. At that point, the wait set variable is updated to contain only callback handles corresponding to the first message available in each queue. The executor then takes all the ready callbacks from wait set and executes them based on their priority. Once all the executions are finished, the wait set is once again reconstructed and passed to the blocking wait function. If there is no available data in the rmw queues or the timer has not triggered, the executor blocks with a timeout and yields the CPU resource to other tasks in the system. The priority of a callback in an executor is decided on two levels: • Callback type: Different callback types have different priority levels. The execution order from the first (highest priority) to the last (lowest priority) is timer callback, subscription callback, service callback, and client callback. • Registration order: Among callbacks with the same type, the earlier the callback is registered to the executor, the earlier (higher priority) it is executed. ROS2 executor also has callback group concept. Every callback is in a callback group, which can be one of two types: Reentrant (default) or Mutually Exclusive. Callbacks in a Mutually Exclusive callback group cannot run simultaneously with another instance of itself or other callbacks in the same group while callbacks in a Reentrant callback group do not have any restriction. It is worth noting that the executors run on top of the operating system, therefore they are dependent on 12 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Figure 5.1: ROS2’s scheduling algorithm the CPU resources assigned by the operating system. Users can assign one or more executors to an operating system thread, and assign priority to this thread to give the executor with critical callbacks higher priority than other executors. However, because the wait set update function is only thread-safe to a certain extent, users cannot have two executors in two separate threads sharing the same callback. For the Linux operating system, users can also choose different scheduling policies such as SCHED FIFO, SCHED RR, and SCHED DEADLINE, and assign priority with levels from 0 to 99 to the threads. With the unique scheduling policy above, the C++ executor has several limitations: 1. It does not support priority setting for the callbacks. The priority between different callback types is fixed. This can lead to resource starvation for the callback types with low priority. 2. The executor itself is non-preemptive, although this problem can be partly addressed by assigning executors to the preemptive threads of the operating system. 3. Only one message per callback is considered for each iteration. Even if there are multiple messages from the same topic are available, only the first one is executed by the executor until it updates the wait set again. This can cause priority inversion as a high-priority backlogged callback have to wait for multiple processing iteration of the executor that executes other lower-priority callbacks. 4. It does not have predictable end-to-end latency. The period between two polling points (when wait set is updated) is dynamic and based on the total execution time of all the callbacks between those two points. A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 13 Overall, the default C++ executor in ROS2 is unpredictable due to its non-preemptive and unique priority assignment as well as non-periodic polling points. 5.2 Micro-ROS Scheduling (C executor) The C executor, even though belongs to the Micro-ROS project, can run with other ROS2 layers thanks to the composable software architecture of ROS2. The scheduling algorithm of the C executor can be seen in Figure 5.2. For each iteration, the executor starts by adding all the handles to a set. The adding order of these handles will determine the execution order of their callbacks. The executor then waits for new data using a wait set variable similar to the C++ executor. Once the wait set is updated with callbacks that have new data, the executor checks if the trigger condition is satisfied. If the trigger condition is not satisfied, the iteration will end and the executor will go to sleep. The trigger condition is defined by the user before run time with four possible options: • All: Trigger if all callbacks have new input data. By combining with the DDS QoS settings, users can synchronize high-frequency callbacks with the lowest frequency callback. • Any: Trigger if at least one of the callbacks has new input data. This is the behavior of the default C++ executor. • One: Trigger if one specific user-defined callback has new input data. Users can use a specific callback to synchronize all callbacks with different frequencies. • Custom: Trigger if the custom user-defined condition is satisfied. If the trigger condition is satisfied, depending on the user setting, the executor can either read all the input data before executing all the callbacks (LET semantics) or read the input data of one callback and execute it sequentially (default semantics). For each callback, users can also set if they want the callback to be executed every time the execute function is called (ALWAYS option) or only when there is a new message (ON NEW DATA). Users have the option to run the executor once, continuously, or periodically. If the executor runs periodically, it will sleep after it finishes one iteration until the next period starts. If the executor runs continuously, it will start the next iteration right after it finishes the current one. These two options are suitable for two different scenarios, the continuous executor is more suitable for an event-driven application, while the periodic executor, when combined with LET semantics, provides a more predictable execution for a periodic application. It improves predictability (for both time and data) by adding options for a periodic executor and LET semantics. 3. It also improves predictability by limiting the use of dynamic memory allocation only during initialization. 4. It separates the callback activation semantics from the application code. By checking activation conditions at the executor level, it reduces the number of callback instances. As a result, the callback runtime overhead is also reduced, especially for high-frequency callbacks. However, several problems remain: 14 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Figure 5.2: Micro-ROS’s scheduling algorithm 1. The LET semantics are not implemented fully. For example, the C executor does not have synchronized output write, and the data read can be preempted or blocked by other higherpriority threads. 2. It still processes one message per callback per execution iteration. 3. It does not provide C++ API. Therefore, it cannot be used with many open-source ROS2 packages. The first problem is specifically related to the LET semantics in the current Micro-ROS executor. We will explore this problem in more detail in the next chapter. However, it is not fully compliant with the LET paradigm’s principles, as some violations are observed in certain scenarios. In this chapter, we will first revisit the LET concept and present what is implemented in the C executor of ROS2/Micro-ROS, then we will identify the current issues with the ROS2/Micro-ROS’s LET executor. 6.1 Mapping the LET Paradigm onto current ROS2/MicroROS constructs As outlined in 2.4, an application in LET paradigm consists of periodic tasks, which produce and consume data. For each task, input is read at the beginning of the period, and output is sent precisely X units of time after reading the input, where X denotes the task’s Logical Execution Time (LET). The flow of data through a sequence of tasks defines a task chain. In ROS2/Micro-ROS, the mapping of LET concepts to ROS constructs is as follows: • A task is represented as a callback, executed by a periodic executor. A callback can be a subscriber callback, service callback, client callback, or timer callback. For subscriber, service, and client callback, data is consumed and published over DDS topics using publishers, clients, and servers. For timer callback, time-triggered events are consumed and data is published over DDS topics using publishers, clients, or servers. • ROS2/Micro-ROS does not enforce periodic release of callbacks, even in their LET implementation. Therefore, tasks are not necessarily periodic. However, the C executor provides the option to define a periodic execution of the executor. If that option is used, then the task period is equivalent to the period of the executor that executes the callback. • The notion of logical execution time does not exist in ROS2/Micro-ROS. • In the C executor, there is an option to read callback input at the beginning of each executor iteration. This option, when combined with the executor’s periodic option, allows the executor to read the callbacks’ input at the beginning of each executor period. 16 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 6.2 Implementation of LET in the current Micro-ROS executor In Micro-ROS, a single-threaded executor is responsible for reading input, executing callbacks, and writing output. Input read is performed at the start of the executor period and consists of the following steps: 1. Wait Set Initialization: Initialize a wait set in the executor with the execution of rclc executor prepare(). 2. Wait Set Configuration: This step reconstructs the wait set with the relevant callback handles in the executor. The wait set is cleared using rcl wait set clear(), and handles associated with the callbacks are added to the wait set through rclc add handles to waitset(). 3. Blocking Wait: The executor enters a blocking state by invoking rcl wait(), waiting for new data or a timeout condition. For subscribers, services, or clients, ”new data” signifies the availability of data within the associated DDS queue. For timers, ”new data” implies that the timer count has reached or exceeded the timer’s trigger time. The rcl wait() updates the executor’s wait set based on which callbacks have new data. 4. Data Availability Check: The executor conducts a check in its wait set for new data through rclc check for new data(). If any callbacks within the wait set have received new data, the data available flag is set accordingly. 5. Trigger Condition Evaluation: The executor’s trigger function is invoked to assess whether the trigger condition has been met. This assessment is based on the data availability status of the callbacks. 6. Data Acquisition: If the trigger condition is satisfied, the process proceeds to rclc take new data(). During this step, for each callback that has received new data, one data item is copied from the DDS queue to the executor for further processing. This step does not apply to timer callback as timer does not have any data in the DDS queue. After input is read, the executor proceeds to execute the respective callbacks using rclc execute() function. For all user-defined callbacks, excluding timers, they are stored within the executor and invoked directly via rclc execute(). Timers, on the other hand, have their callbacks stored within the timer objects in the rcl library. Timers are invoked during the rclc execute() through the rcl’s rcl timer call() function, which also updates the timer’s triggered time to align with its next period. During callback execution, if there is any output, it is written using rcl publish() for publishers, rcl send request() for clients and rcl send response() for servers. 6.3 Issues With the Current LET Executor Implementation As mentioned in the previous chapter, the Micro-ROS executor implements the LET semantics but there remain several limitations. Among those, we will focus on its LET-specific issues as follows: • Issue 1: If the user sets the timeout of rcl wait() to be greater than zero, new input can be read later than the start of the executor period. This is a violation of LET’s input read principle that input reads must happen at the beginning of the task period. An example is shown in Fig. 6.1. In this example, the executor has a rcl wait() timeout of 3 ms and operates with a period of 5 ms. Its callback has incoming data with an arrival period of 8 ms. As depicted in the figure, data arrives at times 4 and 12, while the executor period initiates at times 5, 10, and 15. At time 5, as there is new data available, rcl wait() returns immediately to notify the executor of the new data, allowing it to perform input reading A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 17 and callback execution. Then, at time 10, the executor invokes rcl wait() again to await further data. However, an issue arises at time 12, as it has not yet surpassed the rcl wait() timeout. In this scenario, rcl wait() returns, once again notifying the executor of newly arrived data, enabling the executor to read this input and execute the callback. In an ideal LET executor, data should only be read at the precise beginning of the executor period, which should occur exclusively at times 5 and 15 in this case. Figure 6.1: Issue of current LET executor when rcl wait() timeout is non-zero • Issue 2: If callback execution in the same executor is longer than the executor period, the reading of input data of the next period is blocked until the running callback finishes. This is also a violation of LET’s input read principle which requires input to be read at the beginning of the task period. Fig. 6.2 provides a visual representation of this issue. In this example, data arrives at times 4 and 9, while the executor’s period begins at times 5 and 10. The first callback execution takes 7 ms, causing a delay in the start of the executor period by 2 ms. Consequently, the data that arrived at time 9 is read at time 12, rather than at the ideal time of 10, as stipulated by LET principles. An example is illustrated in Fig. 6.3, where Callback 2 input is read later than the initiation of Executor 2’s period due to preemption by Executor 1’s Callback 1 execution. In an ideal LET situation, Executor 2 reads input at the start of its period regardless of Executor 1 execution. 18 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Figure 6.3: Issue of current LET executor when the executor is preempted or delayed by higherpriority thread • Issue 4: There is no definition of callback’s LET, and output data can be published at any time during the callback execution, which violates the LET’s output write principle. For example, a callback that has a publisher and publishes data once in the middle of callback execution and once at the end of callback execution (Fig. 6.4). With a fully LET-compliant executor, both the data is published at the end of the callback’s LET. Figure 6.4: Issue of current LET executor for publishing output • Issue 5: Overrun error is not detected and handled. An overrun error is when the callback execution does not finish by the end of the callback’s LET. Because there is no definition of callback’s LET in the current LET executor, there is no mechanism to detect an overrun error, thus there is no control over when the data will be written in case of an overrun error. Only one message per callback is considered for each iteration. Even if there are multiple messages from the same topic are available, only the first one is executed by the executor until it updates the wait set again. This can cause priority inversion as a high-priority backlogged callback have to wait for multiple processing iteration of the executor that executes other lower-priority callbacks. 4. It does not have predictable end-to-end latency. The period between two polling points (when wait set is updated) is dynamic and based on the total execution time of all the callbacks between those two points. A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 13 Overall, the default C++ executor in ROS2 is unpredictable due to its non-preemptive and unique priority assignment as well as non-periodic polling points. 5.2 Micro-ROS Scheduling (C executor) The C executor, even though belongs to the Micro-ROS project, can run with other ROS2 layers thanks to the composable software architecture of ROS2. The scheduling algorithm of the C executor can be seen in Figure 5.2. For each iteration, the executor starts by adding all the handles to a set. The adding order of these handles will determine the execution order of their callbacks. The executor then waits for new data using a wait set variable similar to the C++ executor. Once the wait set is updated with callbacks that have new data, the executor checks if the trigger condition is satisfied. If the trigger condition is not satisfied, the iteration will end and the executor will go to sleep. The trigger condition is defined by the user before run time with four possible options: • All: Trigger if all callbacks have new input data. By combining with the DDS QoS settings, users can synchronize high-frequency callbacks with the lowest frequency callback. • Any: Trigger if at least one of the callbacks has new input data. This is the behavior of the default C++ executor. • One: Trigger if one specific user-defined callback has new input data. Users can use a specific callback to synchronize all callbacks with different frequencies. • Custom: Trigger if the custom user-defined condition is satisfied. If the trigger condition is satisfied, depending on the user setting, the executor can either read all the input data before executing all the callbacks (LET semantics) or read the input data of one callback and execute it sequentially (default semantics). For each callback, users can also set if they want the callback to be executed every time the execute function is called (ALWAYS option) or only when there is a new message (ON NEW DATA). Users have the option to run the executor once, continuously, or periodically. If the executor runs periodically, it will sleep after it finishes one iteration until the next period starts. If the executor runs continuously, it will start the next iteration right after it finishes the current one. These two options are suitable for two different scenarios, the continuous executor is more suitable for an event-driven application, while the periodic executor, when combined with LET semantics, provides a more predictable execution for a periodic application. The C executor solves some of the C++ executor’s problems. 1. It provides priority setting through the registration order, leading to tighter bounds on callback execution. 2. It improves predictability (for both time and data) by adding options for a periodic executor and LET semantics. 3. It also improves predictability by limiting the use of dynamic memory allocation only during initialization. 4. It separates the callback activation semantics from the application code. By checking activation conditions at the executor level, it reduces the number of callback instances. As a result, the callback runtime overhead is also reduced, especially for high-frequency callbacks. However, several problems remain: 14 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Figure 5.2: Micro-ROS’s scheduling algorithm 1. The LET semantics are not implemented fully. For example, the C executor does not have synchronized output write, and the data read can be preempted or blocked by other higherpriority threads. 2. It still processes one message per callback per execution iteration. 3. It does not provide C++ API. Therefore, it cannot be used with many open-source ROS2 packages. The first problem is specifically related to the LET semantics in the current Micro-ROS executor. We will explore this problem in more detail in the next chapter. A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 15 Chapter 6 Analysis of The LET Implementation in The C Executor The current executor in Micro-ROS has incorporated the LET concept to improve its determinism. However, it is not fully compliant with the LET paradigm’s principles, as some violations are observed in certain scenarios. In this chapter, we will first revisit the LET concept and present what is implemented in the C executor of ROS2/Micro-ROS, then we will identify the current issues with the ROS2/Micro-ROS’s LET executor. 6.1 Mapping the LET Paradigm onto current ROS2/MicroROS constructs As outlined in 2.4, an application in LET paradigm consists of periodic tasks, which produce and consume data. For each task, input is read at the beginning of the period, and output is sent precisely X units of time after reading the input, where X denotes the task’s Logical Execution Time (LET). The flow of data through a sequence of tasks defines a task chain. In ROS2/Micro-ROS, the mapping of LET concepts to ROS constructs is as follows: • A task is represented as a callback, executed by a periodic executor. A callback can be a subscriber callback, service callback, client callback, or timer callback. For subscriber, service, and client callback, data is consumed and published over DDS topics using publishers, clients, and servers. For timer callback, time-triggered events are consumed and data is published over DDS topics using publishers, clients, or servers. • ROS2/Micro-ROS does not enforce periodic release of callbacks, even in their LET implementation. Therefore, tasks are not necessarily periodic. However, the C executor provides the option to define a periodic execution of the executor. If that option is used, then the task period is equivalent to the period of the executor that executes the callback. • The notion of logical execution time does not exist in ROS2/Micro-ROS. • In the C executor, there is an option to read callback input at the beginning of each executor iteration. This option, when combined with the executor’s periodic option, allows the executor to read the callbacks’ input at the beginning of each executor period. 16 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 6.2 Implementation of LET in the current Micro-ROS executor In Micro-ROS, a single-threaded executor is responsible for reading input, executing callbacks, and writing output. Input read is performed at the start of the executor period and consists of the following steps: 1. Wait Set Initialization: Initialize a wait set in the executor with the execution of rclc executor prepare(). 2. Wait Set Configuration: This step reconstructs the wait set with the relevant callback handles in the executor. The wait set is cleared using rcl wait set clear(), and handles associated with the callbacks are added to the wait set through rclc add handles to waitset(). 3. Blocking Wait: The executor enters a blocking state by invoking rcl wait(), waiting for new data or a timeout condition. For subscribers, services, or clients, ”new data” signifies the availability of data within the associated DDS queue. For timers, ”new data” implies that the timer count has reached or exceeded the timer’s trigger time. The rcl wait() updates the executor’s wait set based on which callbacks have new data. 4. Data Availability Check: The executor conducts a check in its wait set for new data through rclc check for new data(). If any callbacks within the wait set have received new data, the data available flag is set accordingly. 5. Trigger Condition Evaluation: The executor’s trigger function is invoked to assess whether the trigger condition has been met. This assessment is based on the data availability status of the callbacks. 6. Data Acquisition: If the trigger condition is satisfied, the process proceeds to rclc take new data(). During this step, for each callback that has received new data, one data item is copied from the DDS queue to the executor for further processing. This step does not apply to timer callback as timer does not have any data in the DDS queue. After input is read, the executor proceeds to execute the respective callbacks using rclc execute() function. For all user-defined callbacks, excluding timers, they are stored within the executor and invoked directly via rclc execute(). Timers, on the other hand, have their callbacks stored within the timer objects in the rcl library. Timers are invoked during the rclc execute() through the rcl’s rcl timer call() function, which also updates the timer’s triggered time to align with its next period. During callback execution, if there is any output, it is written using rcl publish() for publishers, rcl send request() for clients and rcl send response() for servers. 6.3 Issues With the Current LET Executor Implementation As mentioned in the previous chapter, the Micro-ROS executor implements the LET semantics but there remain several limitations. Among those, we will focus on its LET-specific issues as follows: • Issue 1: If the user sets the timeout of rcl wait() to be greater than zero, new input can be read later than the start of the executor period. This is a violation of LET’s input read principle that input reads must happen at the beginning of the task period. An example is shown in Fig. 6.1. In this example, the executor has a rcl wait() timeout of 3 ms and operates with a period of 5 ms. Its callback has incoming data with an arrival period of 8 ms. As depicted in the figure, data arrives at times 4 and 12, while the executor period initiates at times 5, 10, and 15. At time 5, as there is new data available, rcl wait() returns immediately to notify the executor of the new data, allowing it to perform input reading A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 17 and callback execution. Then, at time 10, the executor invokes rcl wait() again to await further data. However, an issue arises at time 12, as it has not yet surpassed the rcl wait() timeout. In this scenario, rcl wait() returns, once again notifying the executor of newly arrived data, enabling the executor to read this input and execute the callback. In an ideal LET executor, data should only be read at the precise beginning of the executor period, which should occur exclusively at times 5 and 15 in this case. Figure 6.1: Issue of current LET executor when rcl wait() timeout is non-zero • Issue 2: If callback execution in the same executor is longer than the executor period, the reading of input data of the next period is blocked until the running callback finishes. This is also a violation of LET’s input read principle which requires input to be read at the beginning of the task period. Fig. 6.2 provides a visual representation of this issue. In this example, data arrives at times 4 and 9, while the executor’s period begins at times 5 and 10. The first callback execution takes 7 ms, causing a delay in the start of the executor period by 2 ms. Consequently, the data that arrived at time 9 is read at time 12, rather than at the ideal time of 10, as stipulated by LET principles. Figure 6.2: Issue of current LET executor when callback execution is longer than executor period • Issue 3: If the executor is preempted or delayed by other high-priority threads (e.g. other executors or applications in the device), the reading of input data is delayed till after the higher-priority threads yield the CPU. It is again a violation of LET’s input read principle. An example is illustrated in Fig. 6.3, where Callback 2 input is read later than the initiation of Executor 2’s period due to preemption by Executor 1’s Callback 1 execution. In an ideal LET situation, Executor 2 reads input at the start of its period regardless of Executor 1 execution. 18 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Figure 6.3: Issue of current LET executor when the executor is preempted or delayed by higherpriority thread • Issue 4: There is no definition of callback’s LET, and output data can be published at any time during the callback execution, which violates the LET’s output write principle. For example, a callback that has a publisher and publishes data once in the middle of callback execution and once at the end of callback execution (Fig. 6.4). With a fully LET-compliant executor, both the data is published at the end of the callback’s LET. Figure 6.4: Issue of current LET executor for publishing output • Issue 5: Overrun error is not detected and handled. An overrun error is when the callback execution does not finish by the end of the callback’s LET. Because there is no definition of callback’s LET in the current LET executor, there is no mechanism to detect an overrun error, thus there is no control over when the data will be written in case of an overrun error. A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 19 Chapter 7 Our Implementation of a LET-compliant Executor In this chapter, we present two proposed solutions aimed at addressing the identified issues with the ROS2/Micro-ROS’s LET executor. These solutions are designed to realize a fully LET-compliant executor. The first solution focuses on supporting exclusively local communication, while the second solution extends the LET executor to handle distributed communication, aligning with the System LET concept

The application will run on a single-core Linux platform. 2. The LET executor is run periodically using the rclc executor spin period() function to execute periodic callbacks. 3. The application only contains Timers, Publishers, and Subscribers (Server and Client may be supported using the same solution as discussed in this document, but as a proof of concept, we limit the scopes to Timers, Publishers, and Subscribers) 4. Each publisher is called by only one callback. To simplify the handling of publisher outputs and avoid the complexity associated with distinguishing between outputs of different callbacks within a single publisher, each publisher is exclusively invoked by a single callback. Identifying the caller from inside the publisher would require users to define unique callback identifiers and provide them as arguments when invoking publish calls. This would over-complicate the implementation as well as the user experience. 5. The composition of the application is defined at compiled time. This includes: • The number of Timers, Publishers, and Subscribers. • Which callback calls a Publisher. • Each callback’s LET. • The number of times a publisher is called in a callback. 20 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 • The executor period 6. No dynamic memory allocation is used after initialization. All dynamic memory allocation should only happen once during the initialization of the system. This constraint is to comply with the current implementation of the C executor, which aims to avoid the unpredictability of dynamic memory allocation. 7. The LET executor is implemented in the rclc library using C language. 7.1.2 Requirements A fully LET-compliant executor has three main components: 1. Input reads must happen at the beginning of the executor period. An input read is defined as the act of checking for new data in the DDS queue, verifying trigger conditions, and if the trigger condition is satisfied, fetching data from the DDS queue to the executor. 2. Output writes must happen at the end of a callback LET, which is user-defined. An output write is defined as the act of publishing data to the appropriate topic in the DDS layer. 3. Overrun errors (i.e. when the callback execution has not finished by the end of its LET) must be detected and handled. Besides the above main three components, the LET-compliant executor also needs to be compatible with ROS2 and Micro-ROS applications: 1. The LET executor must be able to execute multiple callbacks with different LETs. 2. The LET executor must be able to execute a callback that calls multiple publishers. 3. The LET executor must be able to execute a callback that calls one publisher multiple times. 4. The application must be able to run multiple instances of the LET executor and default executor together simultaneously. The example features an executor containing a timer and a subscriber, each with its distinct callback LET. Input Thread It is activated periodically with the period of the executor. Once it is activated, it reads input from the DDS layer and stores it along with a data available flag in an internal buffer inside the executor. For timers, it checks if the timer has been triggered and sets the data available flag for that timer accordingly. After that, it sends a signal to the callback thread to notify inputs have been read successfully. To ensure that the LET executor is not preempted or blocked by other threads or callback executions, the Input Thread is executed at a high priority. However, to prevent its execution from interfering with the Input Thread and Output Thread, the Callback Thread’s priority must always be lower than the Input Thread and Output Thread’s priority. At the start of its period, it waits for the Input Thread to send a signal to notify that it finished reading inputs. It executes the callbacks only when the Input Thread has finished reading the input, new data is available, and the trigger condition is met. For each callback with output data, the Callback Thread writes the data to an internal buffer inside the associated publisher. 22 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Figure 7.2: A component diagram of Solution 1’s design Output Thread The Output Thread is activated at the end of each callback LET. Upon activation, this thread retrieves data from the internal buffers of the relevant publishers—those associated with callbacks whose LETs end concurrently with the Output Thread’s activation. Subsequently, this data is published to the DDS layer. To guarantee that the output can be published exactly at the end of each callback’s LET regardless of the executor’s state at that instant, the Output Thread operates at a high priority (the same priority as the Input Thread). The high priority allows the Output Thread to preempt the Callback Thread if it still executing other callbacks but not the Input Thread, thus ensuring that data are published exactly at the end of callback LET. At the beginning of the executor period, the Input Thread copies data from the DDS layer to the input buffers. If there is no data available for a specific callback, it will clear the content of the corresponding buffer. Once the Input Thread finishes and signals the Callback Thread, the Callback Thread wakes up and executes callbacks with available data in the input buffers. During the callback execution, the Callback Thread copies the output to the corresponding publisher of the executing callback. At the end of each callback LET, the Output Thread wakes up, takes the data out of the corresponding output buffer, and publishes it to the DDS layer. If the Callback Thread is executing callbacks when the Input Thread or the Output Thread wakes up, it will be preempted. 7.2.2 Implementation 7.2.2.1 Input Read When the Input Thread wakes up, its primary task is to perform input reads. Instead of maintaining a single output index, the Output Thread keeps an index for each callback, incrementing it at the end of each callback’s LET. Static memory is allocated at compile-time for global and static variables. Its size remains fixed once the program is compiled and persists throughout the program’s lifetime. Stack memory is utilized for local variables and function call information. It grows and shrinks during run time, therefore we are only interested in its maximum value. Dynamic memory is the memory dynamically allocated by the program by calls to calloc() and malloc() functions in the C language. We can only estimate theoretically through code investigation the usage of dynamic memory. Another potential improvement is to consolidate multiple intermediate topics into a single topic when there are multiple executor periods in a callback LET. In such cases, publishers can append an index at the beginning of the message to indicate the period to which the message belongs. This approach could help optimize memory usage further. Within this metric, our primary interest centers on the input read overhead and the output write overhead as there are minimal changes regarding the callback execution. There are two types of overhead that we want to evaluate: • Runtime Overhead Comparison with Current LET Executor: The runtime overhead introduced by our new LET executor when compared to the existing LET executor is evaluated. It is derived as the difference between the execution times of input read and output write operations for an application running our new LET executor versus the same application running the current LET executor. • Runtime Overhead Comparison with Default LET Executor: This evaluation involves measuring the runtime overhead of our new LET executor when compared to the default LET executor, which typically operates in continuous mode—an approach widely used 62 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 in ROS2/Micro-ROS executors. It is calculated as the difference in execution times for input read and output write operations between an application running our new LET executor and the same application utilizing the default executor. It is worth noting that the total overhead is considerably influenced by the experiment’s duration and the frequency of the executor period. Consequently, we present this data as relative overhead, normalized to the total application runtime duration. We maintain a consistent executor period across most tests, with exceptions for experiments involving varying executor periods. 2. LET Thread Execution Time at each wake-up. In this metric, we focus on quantifying the execution time of the LET Thread during each wake-up event, separately for input read and output write operations. Given the LET Thread’s higher priority compared to the Callback Thread and other system threads, understanding its execution time is important. The execution time of the LET Thread will have a direct effect on the response time of all the lower-priority threads due to preemption or delay from the LET Thread. This measurement therefore is important to understand how long the callback threads are preempted, and therefore how the callbacks’ WCRTs are affected. 9.2.1 Methodology 9.2.1.1 Test Scenarios We use the same test scenarios as in the memory usage evaluation. We also divide the evaluation into two parts: Comparison between two approaches and Scalability tests for Solution 1. 9.2.1.2 Data Collection To measure execution time, clock gettime() function with CLOCK THREAD CPUTIME ID is used to read thread time in a multi-threaded application. If we do not have access to the code (for example, the thread is created by a lower layer), we will read the CPU time of each thread from se.sum exec runtime variable in the \proc\<pid>\task\<tid>\sched virtual file of the application Linux process at the end of the application. To decide the point to take the timestamps for execution time measurements, we need to define which parts of the code belong to input read, callback execution, and output write. • Input Read: 1. Solution 1: • To measure the total input overhead, we measure the total execution time of input read with the LET executor and the total execution time of input read with the default execution. The total input overhead is the difference between these two measurements. • To measure the total output overhead, we measure the total execution of the LET thread for writing output, then add the total execution time of copying the data to the internal buffer inside the publishers. Finally, because both the LET executor and the default executor publish the data to the DDS layer once, we subtract the total execution time of publishing the data to the DDS layer from the previous sum. • To measure the execution time of the LET thread at each wake-up, we read the thread time at each wake-up and right before it goes to sleep. The execution time is the difference between these two readings. 2. Solution 2: Because only the output intermediate node is implemented, we only measure the code overhead for output write. The overhead for input read should be similar as the implementation A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 63 is the same between the input intermediate node and the output intermediate node (the only difference is the number of intermediate publishers and subscribers). • To measure the total output overhead, we first measure the total execution time of the executor of the output intermediate node. We then measure the total execution time of the DDS threads with the LET executor and the total execution time of the DDS threads with the default executor. Finally, we add the difference between these DDS threads’ total execution times to the total execution time of the output intermediate nodes’ executors. This method does not give the exact extra time of each output intermediate node at the DDS layer but can give us a rough idea of how much overhead it created. 9.2.1.3 Test Setup We use the parameter in Table 9.5 as the base for our tests. We learn that the choice of callback LET does not make any impact on the overhead of the new LET executor, the number of timers makes a minimal impact on the overhead, while the message size, the number of publishers, the number of subscribers, and the executor period all have significant impact on the overhead. The DDS vendors have been working on different ways to minimize the runtime overhead of the publishing operation, including a zero-copy mechanism for intra-process communication. The priority queue and mechanism to associate callback IDs with the callbacks can be implemented more efficiently to reduce runtime overhead when there is no data available. Currently, we implement a priority queue using a linked list and use brute force to find the callback associated with a callback ID. Determine the number of executors and the callback distribution between executors: For a real-time system, callbacks within one callback chain should be in the same executor, unless they are spread across multiple processes or machines. Improved Scheduling: callback chains that require lower latency should be added into executor(s) that run on higher-priority thread(s) to reduce the callback WCRT, and as a result, its LET interval. 2. Fine-tuning LET intervals: Users should do extensive static analysis to find the WCRT of each callback and refine the LET intervals to closely match the WCRT. 3. Decrease executor period: Decreasing the executor period can help reduce the gap between the output of a callback with the input of its next callback in the callback chain, therefore reducing the end-to-end latency. Decreasing the executor period can also improve the throughput of the system. However, these improvements come at the cost of greater code overhead and memory consumption. Because of non-zero read and write time, there should be a sufficient gap in time between any instance of input read and output write of executors in a system (assuming single-core). The gap depends on the processing speed of the machine, the scale of the system, and the size of the transporting messages. For the common applications and machines, the gap should be at least 500µs. 3. For the same reason as above, callback with too low an LET interval may occasionally skipped due to preemption from the input and output thread. Users should take into account the execution time of the input and output threads when calculating the WCRT of a callback if there are a large number of executors in the system or if the expected LET interval is low (in the microseconds range). 4. Also for the above reason, users should limit the number of LET executors in a single-core machine (for example, combine all LET executors with the same priority into one). For a multi-core machine, it is sometimes beneficial to split into multiple executors. Hence, users must exercise careful consideration of memory costs when configuring LET executors for their applications. In terms of future optimizations, there is potential to reduce memory usage scalability, particularly for low message sizes. This can be achieved by optimizing certain data structures employed in our implementation to have a smaller memory footprint. However, for larger message sizes, the memory consumed by internal buffers becomes unavoidable and cannot be further optimized. As for Solution 2, it’s evident that a significant portion of memory usage stems from the DDS implementation, which is not currently optimized for memory efficiency. Ongoing efforts by DDS vendors, such as the DDS version for Micro-ROS from eProsima, are expected to address this issue. Additionally, in-depth research on how Quality of Service configurations impact memory usage could offer valuable insights for optimizing memory consumption in the context of intermediate nodes. Another potential improvement is to consolidate multiple intermediate topics into a single topic when there are multiple executor periods in a callback LET. In such cases, publishers can append an index at the beginning of the message to indicate the period to which the message belongs. This approach could help optimize memory usage further. It is worth noting that the total overhead is considerably influenced by the experiment’s duration and the frequency of the executor period. Consequently, we present this data as relative overhead, normalized to the total application runtime duration. We maintain a consistent executor period across most tests, with exceptions for experiments involving varying executor periods. 2. LET Thread Execution Time at each wake-up. In this metric, we focus on quantifying the execution time of the LET Thread during each wake-up event, separately for input read and output write operations. Given the LET Thread’s higher priority compared to the Callback Thread and other system threads, understanding its execution time is important. The execution time of the LET Thread will have a direct effect on the response time of all the lower-priority threads due to preemption or delay from the LET Thread. This measurement therefore is important to understand how long the callback threads are preempted, and therefore how the callbacks’ WCRTs are affected. 9.2.1 Methodology 9.2.1.1 Test Scenarios We use the same test scenarios as in the memory usage evaluation. Solution 1: • To measure the total input overhead, we measure the total execution time of input read with the LET executor and the total execution time of input read with the default execution. The total input overhead is the difference between these two measurements. • To measure the total output overhead, we measure the total execution of the LET thread for writing output, then add the total execution time of copying the data to the internal buffer inside the publishers. Key takeaways from our findings include the following considerations: • Scalability: Memory consumption and runtime overhead scales linearly with the number of callbacks, publishers, and message size, therefore users should aim to minimize the number of ROS2 entities and their message size. • Executor Period: Choosing a low executor period has a trade-off between higher runtime overhead and memory consumption versus lower end-to-end latency and the ability to handle higher data rates. • LET Thread Execution Time Significance: Input read and output write execution times are not negligible, therefore users should take them into account when calculating callback’s WCRT. Based on these takeaways and the details of our implementation, we will provide detailed guidelines on the practical utilization of our new LET executor in the next chapter. 82 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 Chapter 10 Guidelines to use LET-compliant Executor Based on the insights from the performance analysis of our LET executor, in this chapter, we provide a comprehensive guide for configuring and deploying the LET executor within real-time ROS2 applications. We begin with a step-by-step setup guide to facilitate the integration of the LET executor. Subsequently, we offer guidance on choosing the most suitable configuration options for the user’s application. Finally, we present some considerations for fine-tuning and optimizing the LET executor, enabling users to strike the ideal balance between time and data determinism, throughput, and latency in their ROS2 systems. By offering practical insights and guidelines, this chapter serves as a valuable resource for users seeking to implement the LET executor effectively. 10.1 When to Use LET Executor A (real-time) system can be split into three classes: 1. Real-time part that requires low latency and time predictability (e.g. Emergency Stop) 2. Real-time part that requires exact timing of when an action will be taken, requiring not just an upper bound but also a lower bound of the response time and end-to-end latency. (e.g. control system requiring low jitter) 3. Non-real-time part (e.g. GUI) It is recommended to use different types of executors for each class. In particular, the default executor should be used for class 1 and class 3, while the LET-compliant executor is suitable for class 2. The two types of executors can run together without any implication on each other performance except for the preemption of a lower-priority thread by a higher-priority thread. Considerations regarding choosing priority are discussed in Section 10.3. 10.2 Guide to Set Up LET Executors for ROS2/Micro-ROS Applications This section provides a step-by-step guide on how to configure and use the new LET executor. First, to get the full effect of the LET Executor, the users should use a Real-Time Operating System. For ROS2, users can use Linux with PREEMPT RT patch, QNX or VxWorks operating system. For Micro-ROS, the supported RTOS for microcontrollers are FreeRTOS, Nuttx, and Zephyr depending on the microcontroller. For more information on how to set up and configure A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 83 the lower layers for a real-time system, the users can refer to guides from ROS2 Real-Time Working Group 1. Once the users have the environment set up, the following steps should be taken to configure the LET Executor. The APIs used for each step are documented in 7.6. 1. Creates and initializes the timers, subscribers and publishers with the necessary parameters. 2. Write the application code. For the publishers that are used in LET executor, the LET semantics should be passed to the publishers’ call. 3. Create and initialize the executors. For the LET executors, also set its semantics to LET, and define its period. These two parameters must be defined for LET executors before adding the callbacks and publishers to the LET executors as they will be used to determine the buffer size for the data. 4. Add the callbacks to the executors. For LET executors, users also need to define the callback LET (for both timers and subscribers) and message size (for subscribers). 5. Add the publishers to the LET executors. Define the callback that calls each publisher, how many times each publisher is called by a callback, and the message size of each publisher. 6. (Optional) Finalize the executors, subscribers, timers, publishers, and nodes. Once initialized, the application configuration should not be changed, else the users need to go through the setup steps again. 10.3 Configuration Guidelines for LET Executors In this section, we will provide some guidelines on how to determine the best configuration for the LET executor. 1. Determine the number of executors and the callback distribution between executors: For a real-time system, callbacks within one callback chain should be in the same executor, unless they are spread across multiple processes or machines. Executing callbacks from a callback chain in one executor has the following advantages and disadvantages: • Provide simpler control over scheduling for the callback chain. As the callbacks in a callback chain usually are executed with the same priority and period, grouping all of them in an executor reduces the complexity in setting the priority and period of their executor. • With a LET executor, the end-to-end latency of the callback chain is not only predictable but also constant (no jitter) because all callbacks in the callback chain are executed within the same period. • However, the end-to-end latency can be harder to optimize as there is always a gap between the end of the callback’s LET to the start of the next executor period. 2. Determine the priority of all the executors as well as other tasks in the system: To establish the priority hierarchy within the system, we take into account the safety-critical nature of callback chains executed by each executor. Although the LET Threads within LET executors inherently operate at a high priority, in our Linux implementation, priorities exceeding 90 are exclusively reserved for safety-critical tasks and executors. For the LET executors, the lower its priority is, the larger the callback’s response time (and callback’s LET), and the larger the end-to-end latency is. Consequently, users should strive to set the 1https://ros-realtime.github.io/Guides/guides.html 84 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 LET executors’ priority as high as possible within the allowable limit based on their safetycritical significance. This strategic prioritization not only minimizes callback response times and LET but also reduces the end-to-end latency of the callback chains. 3. Determine the callback LETs: • Do a test run without using the LET executor to determine the WCET of each callback and task in the system. Only tasks and callbacks that have priority equal to or higher than the LET executor’s priority are concerned. • Do a WCRT analysis for each callback in the LET executor, then set the callback’s LET to be higher than its WCRT. 10.4 Optimizing the LET Executor Performance As mentioned in Section 2.4 and showed in experiments results in Chapter 9, using LET-compliant executor will increase the end-to-end latency of its callback chains. There are a few things that users can do to mitigate this impact on the latency increase: 1. Improved Scheduling: callback chains that require lower latency should be added into executor(s) that run on higher-priority thread(s) to reduce the callback WCRT, and as a result, its LET interval. 2. Fine-tuning LET intervals: Users should do extensive static analysis to find the WCRT of each callback and refine the LET intervals to closely match the WCRT. 3. Decrease executor period: Decreasing the executor period can help reduce the gap between the output of a callback with the input of its next callback in the callback chain, therefore reducing the end-to-end latency. Decreasing the executor period can also improve the throughput of the system. However, these improvements come at the cost of greater code overhead and memory consumption. The LET-compliant executor does not always guarantee predictability in timing and data flow. Here are a few considerations to avoid these situations: 1. LET executor must be periodic. 2. Because of non-zero read and write time, there should be a sufficient gap in time between any instance of input read and output write of executors in a system (assuming single-core). The gap depends on the processing speed of the machine, the scale of the system, and the size of the transporting messages. For the common applications and machines, the gap should be at least 500µs. 3. For the same reason as above, callback with too low an LET interval may occasionally skipped due to preemption from the input and output thread. Users should take into account the execution time of the input and output threads when calculating the WCRT of a callback if there are a large number of executors in the system or if the expected LET interval is low (in the microseconds range). 4. Also for the above reason, users should limit the number of LET executors in a single-core machine (for example, combine all LET executors with the same priority into one). For a multi-core machine, it is sometimes beneficial to split into multiple executors. A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 85 Chapter 11 Conclusion Recap of Research Questions: Before summarising the work in this thesis, it is necessary to revisit the research questions from Chapter 4. There are three main research questions, which are: • RQ1: What are the potentials and limitations when using the ”Micro-ROS” C executor in ROS 2 in terms of timing and data determinism? • RQ2: How can a Logical Execution Time (LET-compliant executor be effectively implemented in Micro-ROS? • RQ3: What are the guidelines and recommendations for configuring and utilizing the MicroROS executor to optimize performance for achieving time and data determinism versus achieving high throughput and low latency? Summary of Answers and Findings: To answer RQ1, in Chapter 5 we conducted a detailed analysis of the C++ executor in ROS2 and the C executor in Micro-ROS. We highlighted the improvements brought by the C executor, such as lower bounds on callback execution times through user-defined callback priority setting and enhanced predictability in time and data flow thanks to the introduction of the LET concept along with a periodic executor. However, we also recognized its limitations, including the remaining problem of priority inversion and incomplete LET semantics. We then identify five issues with the current implementation of the LET semantics in the C executor in Chapter 6, which are non-zero wait timeouts, blocked input read, preemption or delay of input reads, non-deterministic output write, and undetected overrun errors. RQ2 was tackled in Chapter 7, where we introduced two solutions to implement a fully LETcompliant executor. The first solution focuses on local communication within a device and employs internal buffers in the executor and publisher to store data. The second solution extended support to distributed communication by adding intermediate nodes to synchronize data communication between callbacks. We also proposed three options to handle overrun errors. Our proof-of-concept implementations satisfied our defined requirements (Section 7.1), and we acknowledged the advantages and disadvantages of each solution. We concluded that the ideal approach would combine elements of both solutions, utilizing Solution 1 for local communication and Solution 2 exclusively for distributed communication. A performance analysis in Chapter 9 assessed the memory usage and runtime overhead of our solutions and shows that the memory and runtime overhead of our new LET executor depends on multiple parameters, including the number of callbacks (subscriber, timer) and output entities (publisher), the executor period and callback LETs, and the message size. Finally, RQ3 is answered in Chapter 10, in which based on our performance analysis, we provided a step-by-step guide on how to set up and configure our new LET executor within an 86 A Logical Execution Time-compliant Executor for ROS2 actual ROS2 system. We also offered practical considerations for optimization. In summary, our project effectively addresses all posed research questions. The thorough breakdown of the current executor implementations provides a deeper comprehension of its operation. The introduction of our LET-compliant executor, when integrated with the default executor, presents a path towards achieving a fully real-time and predictable ROS2 system, subject to certain conditions mentioned in Section 10. Moreover, this project lays a foundation for future enhancements in ROS2 executor design, aligning with the ROS community’s vision of refining ROS2 execution management.
